package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of Envoy Proxy contain a denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability (CVE-2022-29225) in the Brotli and GZip decompression filters. Attackers can exploit this by sending highly-compressed files that decompress to extremely large sizes, causing unbounded memory allocation, performance degradation, and potential process crashes.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when Envoy Proxy receives HTTP requests with Brotli-compressed payloads and the Brotli decompression filter is enabled
execution_context.file_location: http_filters configuration referencing type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.compression.brotli.decompressor.v3.Brotli (Envoy core source code, decompression filter implementation)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving an HTTP request with a Brotli-compressed payload, the code decompresses the payload in a loop, appending all decompressed data to a buffer without enforcing a maximum output size, resulting in unbounded memory allocation and potential process crash.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code allows unbounded memory allocation based on attacker-controlled compressed input, which is a classic vector for denial-of-service attacks. There is no check or enforcement of a maximum decompressed output size.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal decompression routines should enforce strict output size or resource limits to prevent resource exhaustion. In this case, the absence of such limits allows a single request to consume all available memory.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate decompression of large files may occur, but always with enforced output size or memory limits to prevent resource exhaustion.
key_indicators: No output buffer size or decompressed data limit enforced in decompression logic
Memory allocation directly proportional to decompressed size, not input size
Absence of safeguards against decompression bombs

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a Brotli-compressed file (Brotli bomb) that decompresses to a very large size.
attack_chain.leads_to: File is sent to Envoy Proxy via HTTP request.

attack_chain.action: Envoy Proxy receives the HTTP request and, due to its configuration, invokes the Brotli decompression filter.
The Brotli decompression filter decompresses the payload into an unbounded buffer, consuming excessive memory.
attack_chain.leads_to: System memory exhaustion, performance degradation, or process crash (DoS).

behavioral_signatures: Sudden, unusually large memory allocation during HTTP request processing involving Brotli or GZip decompression
Decompression of Brotli or GZip payloads with no output size or memory limit enforced
Envoy Proxy process crash or restart following receipt of large compressed payloads
Spike in memory usage correlated with specific HTTP requests containing compressed data
network_indicators: Inbound HTTP requests with unusually large Brotli-compressed payloads
Repeated HTTP requests from a single source containing highly-compressed data
Patterns of requests that trigger memory spikes or process instability
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Envoy Proxy configurations for enabled Brotli or GZip decompression filters. Use system and application monitoring to detect sudden spikes in memory usage during HTTP request processing. Inspect logs for process crashes or restarts following large compressed payloads. Employ software composition analysis (SCA) tools to identify vulnerable Envoy versions and flag configurations that enable decompression without output size or memory limits. Correlate network traffic with resource exhaustion events to identify potential exploitation attempts.
